summary: A revision of the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, the way one computer asks another to send or receive files. It came out of months of discussion in RFCs and a committee meeting at BBN, and changes the previous official version while keeping its overall structure. It was replaced by RFC 765.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computers need a polite way to hand files to each other. This paper is the rulebook for that, updated after many people argued over the details.

questions: how did ftp work on the arpanet
subtitle: The 1973 revision of the ARPANET file transfer protocol, with a control channel, data connections and transfer modes.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the ARPANET stored files in very different ways, and the previous official FTP version needed rework after months of discussion.
tldr.mechanism: A user process sends FTP commands over TELNET connections to a server, and the server opens a separate data connection to move the file in a chosen type, structure and mode.
tldr.outcome: This version was to move to Socket 3 on 1 February 1974, replacing the old one. It was later obsoleted by RFC 765 and updated by RFC 614 and RFC 640.

today: RFC 542 was obsoleted by RFC 765 and updated by RFC 614 and RFC 640, so it is a historical version of FTP.

sections.title: Goals and the FTP Model
sections.content:
The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) moves files between Hosts, including TIPs, on the ARPANET. Its objectives are to promote file sharing, to encourage indirect use of remote computers through programs, to shield users from differences in file storage systems, and to transfer data reliably and efficiently.

A user-side protocol interpreter (PI) sends commands over TELNET connections to a server-PI, which replies and directs a data transfer process (DTP). The file moves over a separate data connection that need not exist all the time. A user can also arrange a transfer directly between two servers, with control passing only through the user.
sections.plainLanguage: One line is for talking and another line is for sending the file. A helper can even set up a transfer between two faraway computers.

sections.title: Data Types, Structure and Connections
sections.content:
FTP lets the user pick how data is represented. The types are ASCII (the default), EBCDIC, Image, and Local byte with a stated byte size. ASCII and EBCDIC take a second format parameter: Non-print (the default), TELNET format controls, or Carriage Control (ASA). Files may have file-structure (no records, the default) or record-structure.

Each side has default data sockets. The data byte size defaults to 8 bits. The server normally opens the data connection, and the SOCK command can name another data socket. The server must close it in listed cases, such as an ABORT command or the TELNET connections closing.
sections.plainLanguage: The computers agree whether the file is text or raw bits, and whether it is one long piece or many records, so nothing gets scrambled.

sections.title: Transmission Modes and Restart
sections.content:
There are three modes. Stream is the default and sends bytes with little processing. Block sends data blocks with a header holding a byte count and descriptor codes: 128 for end of record, 64 for end of file, 32 for suspected errors and 16 for a restart marker. Compressed replaces repeated bytes and filler with short counts.

FTP does not detect bits lost or scrambled, and leaves that to lower layers. For gross system failures it provides a restart procedure in Block and Compressed modes: the sender inserts markers, the receiver records them, and the user can resume with the REST command followed by the interrupted transfer command.
sections.plainLanguage: Files can be sent plainly, in labelled chunks, or squeezed smaller. Bookmarks in the chunks let a broken transfer pick up where it stopped.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
Commands are TELNET strings. Access control commands include USER, PASS, ACCT, REIN and BYE. Parameter commands include BYTE (1 through 255), SOCK, PASV, TYPE, STRU and MODE. Service commands include RETR, STOR, APPE, ALLO, REST, RNFR, RNTO, ABOR, DELE, LIST, NLST, SITE, STAT, HELP and NOOP. Experimental commands begin with an X.

Replies start with a three-digit code. The first digit gives the kind of answer: 2xx is positive, 3xx needs more input, 4xx is an unsuccessful request and 5xx is an incorrect or illegal command. Multi-line replies repeat the code on the last line.

The preface notes that the many incompatibilities with the old version made a phased rollout hard. The new version was assigned temporary Socket 21, and on 1 February 1974 it was to move to Socket 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends short word-commands like fetch or store, and the server answers with a number that tells a program whether it worked.

items.label: Positive
items.desc: Positive acknowledgment of a previous command or other successful action.

items.label: Incomplete
items.desc: More specification or input is needed before activity can proceed.

items.label: Unsuccessful
items.desc: The request was correct but the server could not fulfil it.

items.label: Incorrect
items.desc: Illegal or inconsistent command; it was ignored.

references.text: File Transfer Protocol, RFC 354, the previous official version.
